method: Flesch-Kincaid grade with a transparent vowel-group syllable heuristic; estimated age = grade + 5, floored at zero. Count sentences using terminal punctuation. Exact measured corpora included. This is a rough editorial screen, not a learner assessment. Teacher-only text excluded.

corpora.text: I can put a short story in order with my group. I can show the start, change and end. I can use my part or cue. I can keep my own choice in my arts log. Choose to act, speak, point or direct. Keep a clear space. Stay in your own space. This is a made-up story. You can sit. Our story is The new den. Start: We want a den in a big space. Change: The space is too small. End: We choose a small den. Point to the end. Watch three still poses. One: Point at a big space. Two: Hold hands close. Look and pause. Three: Point at a small den. Hold each pose for three slow counts. Pick a role in our group. Choose a pose for each part. Use Start, Next, End as cues. Try all three in order. Which pose shows the change? In your group, make three parts. Choose your role and one idea. Try the story twice. Keep the order: start, change, end. In your book or arts log, draw or tell your three parts. Add: My choice was ___. Show the three parts to a partner or the adult. The watcher says: I saw ___ first. Did the new plan come last? Choose one thing to keep. Sit and put books away with care. Arts log: My role was ___. My choice was ___. Our story went first ___, next ___, last ___. Next time I will ___. A shape you hold still. A sign to start or stop. What comes first, next and last. The part you do in a group.

Use the three story parts. Pick a role with the adult. Choose one pose or cue. Try the three parts with help. Tell or point to your own choice. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Agree your role and one idea. Make the start, change and end. Use one cue for each part. Try twice and keep the order. Keep your own choice in your arts log. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Use the same three-part task. Test a spoken cue and a silent cue. Choose which helps the order most. Say why and keep that choice. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

The group point at a big space. Next they show a small space with their hands. Last they point to a new small den. They hold each pose for three counts. What comes first? What comes last? How can a still pose show the change? A voice says Start, Next, End. The group make one pose at each cue. In the middle a helper says, Can we change it? The group point to a new plan. Which word helps the group change pose? Which cue could help our group? I notice ___. I could use ___ in my own scene because ___. These are invented class models. They are not pupil work.

Point wide. Say: We want a den. Hold for three counts. Hands close. Pause. Say: The space is small. Ask: Can we change it? Make a small roof with hands. Point to the three parts. Say: Start, change, end. I kept that order. Choose your role. Try a short scene. Change one thing. The adult model is an example. Your arts log must show your real choice.

Sequence a short drama with a group. I can show the start, change and end. I can use my part or cue. I can keep my own choice in my arts log. pose: A shape you hold still. cue: A sign to start or stop. order: What comes first, next and last. role: The part you do in a group. Use a made-up story. Keep your own space. Stop on the open hand. You can sit, stay silent or direct. You may share with just the adult.

I can use a cue to help my group tell our story. I can show our story in order. I can use a clear cue or pose. I can say what we changed. Find our three-part story. Choose your role again. You may change it. Sit or stand in your own clear space. Use the open-hand stop cue. First: We want a den. Next: The space is small. Last: We choose a small den. Put these parts in order. Point to the part we can make clearer. Watch a fast change. It is hard to see. Watch a slow cue and a still pose. Which is clear? I change one thing. I keep the same story order. Agree one change to our group story. Try it once. A watcher points to the change. Keep it or try again. Use kind words: I saw ___. Rehearse your three-part story. Change one cue or pose. Show the story in order. Share with a partner or the adult. In your book or arts log, keep the change and your own part. Watcher: What came first and last? Maker: What did we change? Say one thing to keep. Thank the group. Settle and store your log. My role was ___. We changed ___ to ___. It helped because ___. My next step is ___. A shape you hold still. A sign to start or stop. Try your part before you share. Make one part different.

Use the three story parts. Choose cue or pose as your change. Try it with the adult. Show the parts in order. Point to what you changed. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Rehearse your group story. Change one cue or pose. Share with your chosen watcher. Keep feedback and your own part. Say how the change helped. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Use the same core task. Test two cue timings. Ask which makes the order clear. Choose one and give a reason. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

The group point at a big space. Next they show a small space with their hands. Last they point to a new small den. They hold each pose for three counts. What comes first? What comes last? How can a still pose show the change? A voice says Start, Next, End. The group make one pose at each cue. In the middle a helper says, Can we change it? The group point to a new plan. Which word helps the group change pose? Which cue could help our group? I notice ___. I could use ___ in my own scene because ___. These are invented class models. They are not pupil work.

Rush the three hand poses once. Ask what was hard to see. Repeat with a still close-hand middle pose. Hold for three counts. Use a calm Next cue. Say: I changed one thing. Say: The held pose made the small space clear. Keep the real choice and feedback. Choose your role. Try a short scene. Change one thing. The adult model is an example. Your arts log must show your real choice.

Sequence a short drama with a group. I can show our story in order. I can use a clear cue or pose. I can say what we changed. pose: A shape you hold still. cue: A sign to start or stop. rehearse: Try your part before you share. change: Make one part different. Use a made-up story. Keep your own space. Stop on the open hand. You can sit, stay silent or direct. You may share with just the adult.

I can help devise a short performance that shows a change and a new plan. I can help order four story beats. I can contribute a performance choice. I can record my choice and a next step. Choose a role: mover, voice, narrator or director. You can work seated or use silent gestures. Keep your own clear space. Our story is invented. You do not need a personal story. Story seed: A group plan a show in a wide space. The space becomes smaller. They pause, ask for ideas and change the moves. They finish the show in the smaller space. What changed? What did the group do? Watch two short examples. One uses a narrator. One uses silent cues. Find four beats: plan, change, choice, result. Which feature makes the choice clear? Build four beats as a group. Plan: agree the first idea. Change: show the smaller space. Choice: ask for help or test a small move. Result: show the new plan working. Choose cues and roles. Devise a scene of about 30 to 60 seconds. Keep the four beats in order. Each person contributes a choice. Try it twice. Test one cue, pause or move. In your book or arts log, keep the outline and your part. Show a trial to a peer or the adult. Watcher: What changed? What helped? Maker: Confirm or correct that reading. Choose one feature to improve next lesson. Store the outline and settle. My role and choice were ___. Our four beats were ___. We tested ___ and kept ___ because ___. Next time I will ___. Make a new performance together. One small part of a drama. A sign that tells a performer when to act. Change a plan to fit a new need.

Use the supplied four-beat story. Choose an accessible role. Make one cue, pose or voice choice with help. Rehearse the four beats. Tell or show your choice for the arts log. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Devise four clear beats as a group. Agree roles and safe cues. Try a scene of 30 to 60 seconds twice. Keep one tested feature for a reason. Record your own part and a next step. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Complete the same scene and log. Test two ways to show the choice beat. Ask which helps the audience see the response. Use the feedback to explain your choice. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Four roles plan a show with wide arm moves. The imagined space becomes smaller. A planner asks the group for ideas. They rehearse small arm moves and finish together. A narrator names each change. Which action lets the audience see the problem? Which detail shows how the group responds to change? The group begin with wide poses. A silent palm cue marks a smaller space. One performer pauses and looks at the group. Each offers a small move. They choose one and repeat it together, then hold the final pose. How does this group show a choice without speech? How could we use a pause or repeated move in our own scene? I notice ___. I could use ___ in my own scene because ___. These are invented class models. They are not pupil work.

Show wide arms within your safe space. Say: Our first plan has wide moves. Bring hands close. Say: The imagined space is smaller. Pause. Ask: What could we try? Offer a small hand wave, then repeat it. Hold a final small pose. Say: We changed the move. Our four beats show the new plan. Choose your role. Try a short scene. Change one thing. The adult model is an example. Your arts log must show your real choice.

Compare the two fictional examples. Choose a skill for your own role, such as cue timing or clear narration. Describe a starting point, practise once and note what changes. Keep the comparison, personal skill goal, first trial and a dated reflection in your arts log. Use your own words or confirmed dictated words.

I can refine and share our devised performance using feedback. I can keep a clear change and response in our scene. I can improve one performance feature. I can record feedback and my own contribution. Find your outline and last next step. Choose your role and audience. Use seated, silent or directed performance if needed. Keep clear space and the open-hand stop cue. Recall four beats: plan, change, choice, result. Which beat shows the response to change? Read the real feedback from our trial. Pick one target: cue, pause, voice or move. Watch the choice beat rush past. Now watch a pause, a cue and a small move. What is clearer? I keep the story. I change one feature. I check what the watcher saw. Agree our one target. Try the scene once. The watcher names what they see. Choose whether to keep the change. Confirm roles and cues for sharing. Rehearse the scene with the agreed change. Keep plan, change, choice and result. Share for about 30 to 60 seconds. Ask: What changed? What helped the group? In your book or arts log, keep your role, feedback and next step. Audience: Name the change and the new plan. Makers: Explain one choice you made. Say what helped the audience follow the story. Thank the audience. Store work and settle. My own role and choice were ___. We changed ___ because ___. The watcher noticed ___. This helped or did not yet help because ___. My next step is ___. Practise a scene before sharing it. A comment that helps you review your work. Make a chosen part clearer. The move from one story beat to the next.

Use the four-beat story and an adult cue. Choose one feature to improve. Try it and share privately if you wish. Point to your own contribution. Confirm the feedback and your next step. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Use real feedback to choose one target. Rehearse and keep the four beats. Share with your chosen audience. Check what the audience understood. Record your contribution and next step. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Complete the same share and reflection. Compare your first and later versions. Explain which feature changed the audience reading. Set a clear skill goal for your own role. In your book or arts log, show your own part. I chose ___ because ___. I will try ___ next. You can point, sign, speak, draw or ask an adult to write your words.

Show a rushed choice beat with small hand moves. Repeat with a held pause before the same hand move. Ask the watcher what became clearer. Keep their actual comment. Say: I changed the pause. It helped the choice stand out. My next step is a clear end cue. Choose your role. Try a short scene. Change one thing. The adult model is an example. Your arts log must show your real choice.

Compare your plan with what the viewer saw. Which part showed the change best? Use a real detail. Say why you will keep or change one part. Plan a way to check your next skill goal. Keep your plan, your own part and real feedback. Add your choice and reason. Add a skill goal and a way to check it.
